---
title: "When the posterior will not normalize by hand"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

On the [conjugate-prior page](conjugate-priors.qmd#what-conjugacy-buys-and-what-it-does-not), we multiplied a Bernoulli likelihood by a beta prior and recognized another beta density. That recognition immediately supplied the number needed to make the posterior density integrate to one. But what happens when the product of the likelihood and prior does not have a familiar name?

The posterior still has a perfectly good mathematical definition as long as the relevant integral is finite. We call the parameter-dependent product of the likelihood and prior the **posterior kernel**, and we obtain the posterior density by dividing that kernel by its integral over the parameter space. We call this integral the [**normalizing constant**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html) because dividing by it makes the posterior integrate to one. The difficulty is that we may not know how to evaluate it by hand. For the rest of the computation sequence, we will work with one Provo reading-time model for which this is the case.

We will build the problem from the data upward. First, we reconstruct the path from a reader's eye movement to one passage-level observation. We then compare a normal likelihood with heavier-tailed alternatives and explain the Student-t likelihood and priors used here. Once the model is fixed, we can derive its posterior kernel and approximate the normalizing constant on a grid. The computation comes last because we first need to know which distribution we are trying to approximate.

## From an eye movement to a modeled observation {#provo-data-ladder}

The [Provo Corpus](https://osf.io/sjefs/) contains eye-tracking measurements and predictability norms for 55 English passages. Luke and Christianson ([2018](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4)) describe the resource and its original measurements.

Suppose a reader encounters a word in one of these passages. The corpus treats the region occupied by that word as an *interest area*. A **first fixation duration (FFD)** is the duration, in milliseconds, of the first recorded fixation in that interest area. It is an early and local measure: gaze duration instead sums the fixations in the first run through the word, while total reading time also includes later returns. We choose FFD here because it supplies a relatively direct word-level duration for the present contrast. This choice does not make FFD a complete measure of comprehension.

### Cloze predictability measures {#provo-cloze-measures}

In a **cloze task**, a norming participant sees a passage fragment with the
next word withheld and supplies a continuation. Suppose the withheld target is
*blocked*. An exact spelling match asks whether the response is *blocked*;
a part-of-speech match asks whether the response has the same broad
part-of-speech class as *blocked* even when it is a different word. The source
authors fit models to these response-level matches. `OrthoMatchModel` is the
fitted probability of an exact orthographic, or spelling, match, while
`POSMatchModel` is the fitted probability of a broad part-of-speech match.
These fitted probabilities summarize the source cloze model rather than raw
response proportions.

The corpus also supplies `LSA_Response_Match_Score`. **Latent semantic
analysis (LSA)** represents words in a space learned from patterns of word
co-occurrence; words used in similar contexts tend to lie nearer one another
in that space. The stored score averages the source LSA similarity between the
cloze responses and the target. It is a graded semantic-similarity summary,
whereas the orthographic and part-of-speech measures begin with binary matches.

The source article illustrates the corpus with the fragment “With schools still closed, cars still buried and streets still,” followed by the target verb *blocked*. The target has a position in a particular passage, a part-of-speech label, a word length, the three predictability measures just defined, and one FFD for each reader who fixated it. A reader who skipped the word on the first pass does not contribute a positive FFD.

The prepared table retains the following position-level quantities:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Text_ID`, `Word_Number` | The passage and the word position within that passage. Together they form the stable position key. |
| `Word_Length`, `Word_POS`, `Word_In_Sentence_Number` | The number of letters, the broad part-of-speech class, and the position within the sentence. |
| `OrthoMatchModel` | The fitted cloze probability for an exact orthographic match. |
| `POSMatchModel` | A fitted cloze probability that a response has the target's broad part of speech. |
| `LSA_Response_Match_Score` | The mean source LSA similarity between cloze responses and the target. |
| `mean_log_ffd` | The mean of the logged positive FFDs supplied by readers at this position. It is not the log of the arithmetic mean FFD. |
| `n_fixations` | The number of positive reader-level FFDs entering that mean. |

We will call `mean_log_ffd` the **fixation-contingent mean log FFD**. The name
keeps the selection event inside the estimand: it averages logged durations over
readers who supplied a retained positive fixation at that position. Predictability
may affect both whether a word is fixated and how long the first fixation lasts.
The present response models the second quantity after conditioning on the first;
it contains no zero or placeholder for a skipped word.

| Stage | Quantity retained for this analysis |
|:--|:--|
| Word encounter | A reader may skip the interest area or fixate it. |
| Positive-duration branch | The first positive fixation supplies one FFD. |
| Position summary | Logged FFDs are averaged over the readers on that branch. |
| Passage summary | Position summaries are averaged within noun and verb positions, then subtracted. |

The data ladder has four levels. The source begins with reader-by-word records. The preparation retains complete content-word records with positive FFD, logs each duration, and averages the logged durations over the observed readers at each word position. It then averages those position summaries separately over nouns and verbs within each passage. The final subtraction produces one contrast for each passage.

Thus the prepared passage table contains one summary per passage, derived from 1,593 retained content-word positions. The position summaries were already aggregated across readers, so they are not participant trials. For passage $j$, let $\mathcal N_j$ and $\mathcal V_j$ be its retained noun and verb positions and let $d_{ji}$ be the position-level mean log FFD. We define

$$
y_j=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal N_j|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal N_j}d_{ji}
-
\frac{1}{|\mathcal V_j|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal V_j}d_{ji}.
$$

For instance, the first passage contributes 33 retained positions, including 16 nouns and 13 verbs. Its noun mean is about 5.323 log milliseconds, its verb mean is about 5.216, and its contrast is about 0.108. Exponentiating the contrast gives the ratio of the two geometric means on the millisecond scale. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

## Why aggregate? {#why-aggregate-provo}

The [first treatment of aggregation](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd#what-aggregation-removes) stressed that a summary both answers a question and removes variation. Our current question concerns the distribution of noun--verb contrasts across the 55 passages. We thus calculate one contrast per passage and give each passage one contribution to the model. This prevents passages with more retained noun or verb positions from automatically receiving more weight.

But this choice narrows what we can learn. The passage summaries remove reader variation, word-position variation, reader-by-word-class variation, and information about how precisely each passage contrast was measured. Passages with different noun counts, verb counts, and contributing fixation counts are treated as equally precise observations. A trial-level hierarchical model could represent those sources of variation and answer a richer question. Here we instead focus on the unweighted distribution of the 55 constructed passage contrasts. We represent that distribution with a center and scale.

The resulting analysis assigns equal model weight to 55 passage summaries, each
built from fixation-contingent position means. Reader-level distributions and
their unequal contribution counts have already been removed. Part of speech was
observed rather than assigned, so the noun--verb difference is descriptive. And
the table contains the 55 passages used in the experiment. The corpus
construction process does not supply a sampling frame of English texts.
The model's center therefore concerns the unweighted distribution of these 55
constructed contrasts.

```{r}
#| label: load-provo-passage-target
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/passage-summaries.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
positions <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
N <- length(y)
nu <- 4
response_scale <- sd(y)
prior_mu_sd <- 2 * response_scale
prior_sigma_sd <- 2 * response_scale

stopifnot(
  N == 55L,
  nrow(positions) == 1593L,
  !anyDuplicated(provo$Text_ID),
  all(provo$n_nouns >= 4L),
  all(provo$n_verbs >= 4L),
  all(is.finite(y))
)

data.frame(
  passages = N,
  retained_position_summaries = sum(provo$n_positions),
  mean = mean(y), sd = response_scale, median = median(y),
  minimum = min(y), maximum = max(y),
  proportion_positive = mean(y > 0)
)

positions[
  positions$Text_ID == 1L,
  c(
    "position_id", "Word_Length", "Word_POS",
    "Word_In_Sentence_Number", "mean_log_ffd", "n_fixations"
  )
][1, ]

provo[
  provo$Text_ID == 1L,
  c(
    "Text_ID", "n_positions", "n_nouns", "n_verbs",
    "noun_mean_log_ffd", "verb_mean_log_ffd",
    "noun_minus_verb_log_ffd"
  )
]
```

## Why use a Student-t likelihood? {#a-robust-location-scale-model}

The [Student-t distribution page](../random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution.qmd#construction) used a Student-t distribution as the sampling distribution of a standardized sample mean under a normal model. The role here is different. We use a Student-t distribution as an observation model for the 55 passage contrasts themselves. For fixed observed contrasts, recall that the [likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd#probability-and-likelihood) is the model density viewed as a function of the unknown parameters.

The basic idea is to estimate a common center while allowing an unusually large passage contrast to have less influence than it would under a normal likelihood. More specifically, the passage-level model uses

$$
Y_j\mid\mu,\sigma
\sim t_4(\mu,\sigma),
$$

with

$$
\mu\sim\mathcal N(0,(2s_y)^2),
\qquad
\sigma\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(0,2s_y),
$$

where $s_y$ is the observed [standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd#definition) of the 55 contrasts. Thus both prior scales are computed as `r sprintf("%.6f", prior_mu_sd)`. Because the same outcomes determine the prior scales and enter the likelihood, we interpret the posterior conditionally on this data-dependent calibration; it cannot be presented as an analysis whose prior commitments were specified before these outcomes were inspected. The fixed four degrees of freedom make the observation model less sensitive to an extreme passage than a normal likelihood would be.

This choice makes six assumptions that the notation can otherwise hide:

1. Conditional on $\mu$ and $\sigma$, the passage contrasts are [independent](../foundations/independence.qmd#why-the-characterizations-are-equivalent), so their joint density factorizes.
2. The passages share one location, one scale, and one tail parameter.
3. The distribution is symmetric around $\mu$.
4. The parameter $\sigma$ gives the Student-$t$ scale. With four degrees of
   freedom, the standard deviation equals $\sigma\sqrt{4/(4-2)}$, which is
   larger than $\sigma$.
5. No passage-level predictor explains systematic differences among the contrasts.
6. Each aggregate is treated as observed without a passage-specific measurement-error term.

These assumptions are working simplifications. The histogram below lets us inspect symmetry and tail behavior, but 55 aggregated observations cannot verify conditional independence or recover the variation removed before modeling.

### Why four degrees of freedom? {#why-four-degrees-of-freedom}

We could estimate the degrees of freedom, fix a small value, or use the normal model obtained as the degrees of freedom increase. We choose four for the present analysis because it gives the likelihood finite variance while retaining substantially heavier tails than a normal distribution. Fixing it also leaves only $\mu$ and $\sigma$ unknown, which makes a two-dimensional grid possible. A smaller value would allow still heavier tails; a larger value would approach the normal model. The Provo Corpus does not determine the value four, so the sensitivity calculation below compares it with three, seven, and the normal limit.

### Why these priors? {#provo-priors}

The prior for $\mu$ is centered at zero because zero represents no average noun-minus-verb contrast. Its scale, $2s_y$, is broad relative to the observed contrast distribution. The half-normal prior for $\sigma$ enforces positive scale and downweights implausibly large between-passage dispersion.

A potential worry is that $s_y$ comes from the same outcomes used in the likelihood. That worry is correct. We choose these data-calibrated priors to keep the analysis on the observed scale; they should not be presented as beliefs specified before seeing the data. The following [prior predictive simulation](prior-predictive-distributions.qmd) draws parameters from the priors and then draws a new contrast from the observation model, making their implications visible before the posterior is computed.

```{r}
#| label: check-provo-prior-predictive
set.seed(20261021)
prior_draws <- 10000L
prior_mu <- rnorm(prior_draws, 0, prior_mu_sd)
prior_sigma <- abs(rnorm(prior_draws, 0, prior_sigma_sd))
prior_y <- prior_mu + prior_sigma * rt(prior_draws, df = nu)

rbind(
  data.frame(
    quantity = "mu",
    q025 = quantile(prior_mu, 0.025),
    median = median(prior_mu),
    q975 = quantile(prior_mu, 0.975)
  ),
  data.frame(
    quantity = "new passage contrast",
    q025 = quantile(prior_y, 0.025),
    median = median(prior_y),
    q975 = quantile(prior_y, 0.975)
  )
)
```

The prior predictive contrast is deliberately much wider than the observed passage summaries. This check does not make the prior independent of the data; it shows what the chosen calibration implies.

## Deriving the posterior {#deriving-the-provo-student-t-posterior}

The [posterior-distribution page](posterior-distributions.qmd#updating-a-continuous-parameter) established the rule “likelihood times prior, divided by evidence.” We now apply that rule without dropping the intermediate pieces.

First distinguish the random contrast $Y_j$ from the observed contrast $y_j$. For a general degrees-of-freedom value $\nu$, the location-scale Student-t density is

$$
f(y_j\mid\mu,\sigma,\nu)
=
\frac{
  \Gamma\left((\nu+1)/2\right)
}{
  \Gamma(\nu/2)\sqrt{\nu\pi}\,\sigma
}
\left[
  1+
  \frac{1}{\nu}
  \left(\frac{y_j-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2
\right]^{-(\nu+1)/2}.
$$

Conditional independence turns the 55 density contributions into a product:

$$
L(\mu,\sigma;\mathbf y)
=
\prod_{j=1}^{N}
f(y_j\mid\mu,\sigma,4).
$$

Let $\tau=2s_y$. The two normalized prior densities are

$$
f(\mu)
=
\phi(\mu;0,\tau)
$$

and

$$
f(\sigma)
=
2\phi(\sigma;0,\tau)
\mathbf 1(\sigma>0).
$$

Here $\phi(x;m,s)$ denotes the normal density at $x$ with mean $m$ and standard deviation $s$. The factor of two turns the positive half of the zero-centered normal density into a density that integrates to one.

Thus continuous Bayes' rule gives

$$
f(\mu,\sigma\mid\mathbf y)
=
\frac{
  \left[\prod_{j=1}^{N}f(y_j\mid\mu,\sigma,4)\right]
  \phi(\mu;0,\tau)
  2\phi(\sigma;0,\tau)
  \mathbf 1(\sigma>0)
}{
  \displaystyle
  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
  \int_0^\infty
  \left[\prod_{j=1}^{N}f(y_j\mid\mu',\sigma',4)\right]
  \phi(\mu';0,\tau)
  2\phi(\sigma';0,\tau)
  \,\mathrm d\sigma'\,\mathrm d\mu'
}.
$$

The denominator is where conjugacy fails: the numerator does not match a familiar normalized two-parameter density. But the numerator still defines an unnormalized posterior.

### Jacobians as local stretching {#jacobians-as-local-stretching}

Before writing the posterior in the coordinates used by the computation, we
need to account for a change in scale. The [density-rescaling
page](../random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd#density-rescaling)
established the basic requirement behind a one-dimensional change of variables:
when a coordinate map stretches a short interval, the density must compensate
so that the corresponding interval keeps the same probability. We now apply
that requirement to the positive scale parameter.

Write $\lambda=\log\sigma$, so that $\sigma=\exp(\lambda)$. Recall that a
[derivative is a local rate of
change](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change).
Here $\mathrm d\sigma/\mathrm d\lambda$ is the local stretch factor: it
describes how much a short interval of width $\Delta\lambda$ changes when
mapped to the $\sigma$ scale. For the exponential map,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\lambda}
=
\exp(\lambda)
=
\sigma.
$$

Thus a short interval of width $\Delta\lambda$ maps approximately to an interval of width

$$
\Delta\sigma
\approx
\sigma\,\Delta\lambda.
$$

The picture below shows this stretching directly. Each horizontal segment has
the same width on the $\lambda$ scale: $\Delta\lambda=0.4$. The corresponding
vertical change on the $\sigma$ scale grows as we move to the right. Around a
large value of $\lambda$, the same movement in $\lambda$ therefore covers a
much wider interval of positive $\sigma$ values.

```{r}
#| label: plot-jacobian-stretch
#| fig-cap: "The map sigma = exp(lambda). Equal movements on the log scale produce larger movements on the positive scale as lambda increases."
#| echo: false

jacobian_lambda <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 400L)
jacobian_curve <- data.frame(
  lambda = jacobian_lambda,
  sigma = exp(jacobian_lambda)
)

jacobian_starts <- c(-1.5, -0.25, 1) # dqr-allow: plot-aesthetic
jacobian_intervals <- data.frame(
  lambda_left = jacobian_starts,
  lambda_right = jacobian_starts + 0.4,
  sigma_left = exp(jacobian_starts),
  sigma_right = exp(jacobian_starts + 0.4),
  interval = factor(seq_along(jacobian_starts))
)

ggplot(jacobian_curve, aes(lambda, sigma)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, color = "grey25") +
  geom_segment(
    data = jacobian_intervals,
    aes(
      x = lambda_left, xend = lambda_right,
      y = sigma_left, yend = sigma_left,
      color = interval
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = jacobian_intervals,
    aes(
      x = lambda_right, xend = lambda_right,
      y = sigma_left, yend = sigma_right,
      color = interval
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = jacobian_intervals,
    aes(x = lambda_right, y = sigma_right, color = interval),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", guide = "none") +
  labs(
    x = expression(lambda),
    y = expression(sigma == exp(lambda))
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The probability assigned to the two corresponding intervals must agree:

$$
f_{\lambda}(\lambda)\Delta\lambda
\approx
f_{\sigma}(\sigma)\Delta\sigma
\approx
f_{\sigma}(\sigma)\sigma\Delta\lambda.
$$

Canceling $\Delta\lambda$ gives

$$
f_{\lambda}(\lambda)
=
f_{\sigma}(\sigma)\sigma.
$$

This factor of $\sigma$ is the one-dimensional change-of-variables adjustment, or **Jacobian**, for $\sigma=\exp(\lambda)$. On the log scale, multiplication by $\sigma$ becomes addition of $\log\sigma=\lambda$. Equal-width grid cells in $\lambda$ correspond to increasingly wide intervals in $\sigma$, so the correction preserves their probability mass. The $+\log\sigma$ term does not come from the likelihood or either prior; it comes from expressing posterior mass on the new coordinate scale. The Stan program later lets Stan apply the same correction during its internal transform, so the model code does not add it manually.

We can now write the posterior in the computational coordinates
$\eta=(\mu,\lambda)=(\mu,\log\sigma)$. The unnormalized log posterior is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log\widetilde f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)
={}&\sum_{j=1}^{N}
\left[
\log t_4\!\left(\frac{y_j-\mu}{\sigma}\right)
-\log\sigma
\right]\\
&+\log\phi(\mu;0,2s_y)
+\log 2+\log\phi(\sigma;0,2s_y)
+\log\sigma.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last term is now accounted for before it enters the computation: it is the
log of the local stretch factor derived above.

The mathematical terms and code correspond as follows:

| Mathematical object | Code expression | Role |
|---|---|---|
| $\sum_j\log f(y_j\mid\mu,\sigma,4)$ | `sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma))` | Student-t log likelihood, including the location-scale factor. |
| $\log\phi(\mu;0,2s_y)$ | `dnorm(mu, 0, prior_mu_sd, log = TRUE)` | Location prior. |
| $\log 2+\log\phi(\sigma;0,2s_y)$ | `log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_sigma_sd, log = TRUE)` | Half-normal scale prior for positive $\sigma$. |
| $\log\sigma$ | `eta[2]` | Change-of-variables Jacobian for $\lambda=\log\sigma$. |

## Approximating the posterior on a grid {#provo-posterior-grid}

### The Hessian as local curvature {#hessian-as-local-curvature}

A [matrix represents a linear map, and an inverse matrix reverses that map
when the inverse exists](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#vectors-matrices-and-covariance).
We use both ideas in the local approximation below.

A rectangular grid needs both a center and an extent. We use the posterior
**mode**, the parameter pair at the highest point of the posterior density, as
the center. The optimizer locates this pair by following local slopes.

The [derivative page](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change)
defined a derivative as a local slope. With two parameters, the gradient
collects one slope for each coordinate. The **Hessian** collects the local
rates at which those slopes change: its diagonal entries record curvature
along each coordinate, and its off-diagonal entries record how the slope in
one coordinate changes as the other coordinate changes.

Near a smooth mode, the negative log posterior often resembles a bowl. A
narrow, sharply curved direction rises quickly from the bottom, while a broad,
gently curved direction rises slowly. The Hessian of the negative log
posterior records those local curvatures. Inverting that matrix reverses the
scale: sharp curvature becomes a small local variance and gentle curvature a
large local variance. The resulting **inverse-Hessian approximation** acts
like a local [covariance
matrix](../random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd#definition),
including an off-diagonal term for the local orientation of the two
coordinates.

This approximation describes only the neighborhood of the mode. It can be
misleading for a skewed, multimodal, or weakly identified posterior. We use it
only to propose the grid's extent, then check whether appreciable normalized
weight remains along the grid boundary. Extending seven local standard
deviations in each direction supplies the initial extent; nonnegligible
boundary mass would tell us to widen it even if the optimizer converged.

The contour diagrams show the connection between curvature and local spread.
Each curve joins points at the same increase in negative log density above a
mode at the origin. Closely spaced contours mark a sharp direction; widely
spaced contours mark a gentle direction. Rotating which coordinate is sharp
rotates the long direction of the local covariance approximation.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hessian-curvature
#| fig-cap: "Two quadratic negative-log-density surfaces with different directional curvature. Tighter contours indicate greater curvature and therefore a smaller inverse-Hessian variance in that direction."
#| fig-alt: "Two contour panels centered at zero. In the first, contours are narrow horizontally and broad vertically, showing sharp curvature in mu and gentle curvature in log sigma. In the second, the orientation reverses. The long contour direction corresponds to the larger local variance after the Hessian is inverted."
curvature_grid <- expand.grid(
  mu_offset = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 161L),
  log_sigma_offset = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 161L)
)

sharp_mu <- transform(
  curvature_grid,
  case = "Sharp in mu; gentle in log sigma",
  rise = 0.5 * ((mu_offset / 0.45)^2 + (log_sigma_offset / 1.25)^2)
)
sharp_log_sigma <- transform(
  curvature_grid,
  case = "Gentle in mu; sharp in log sigma",
  rise = 0.5 * ((mu_offset / 1.25)^2 + (log_sigma_offset / 0.45)^2)
)
curvature_examples <- rbind(sharp_mu, sharp_log_sigma)

ggplot(
  curvature_examples,
  aes(mu_offset, log_sigma_offset, z = rise)
) +
  geom_contour(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8), color = "#2C7FB8") + # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(
      mu_offset = 0, # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
      log_sigma_offset = 0, # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
      case = unique(curvature_examples$case)
    ),
    aes(mu_offset, log_sigma_offset),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "#8B1A1A", size = 1.7
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~case) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(
    x = "Change in mu from the mode",
    y = "Change in log sigma from the mode"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank())
```

We chose these fixed quadratic surfaces to expose the geometry. The computation
below obtains local curvature from the fitted Provo posterior and then checks
the resulting grid against posterior mass at its boundaries.

```{r}
#| label: fit-provo-grid-posterior
log_sum_exp <- function(x) {
  maximum <- max(x)
  maximum + log(sum(exp(x - maximum)))
}

weighted_quantile <- function(x, weights, probabilities) {
  ordering <- order(x)
  x <- x[ordering]
  weights <- weights[ordering] / sum(weights)
  cumulative <- cumsum(weights)
  vapply(probabilities, function(probability) {
    x[which(cumulative >= probability)[1]]
  }, numeric(1))
}

log_posterior_eta <- function(eta) {
  mu <- eta[1]
  sigma <- exp(eta[2])
  sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, prior_mu_sd, log = TRUE) +
    log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_sigma_sd, log = TRUE) + eta[2]
}

mode_fit <- optim(
  c(median(y), log(mad(y))),
  function(eta) -log_posterior_eta(eta),
  method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000L)
)
mode_eta <- unname(mode_fit$par)
mode_covariance <- solve(mode_fit$hessian)
grid_sd <- sqrt(diag(mode_covariance))

mu_grid <- seq(mode_eta[1] - 7 * grid_sd[1],
               mode_eta[1] + 7 * grid_sd[1], length.out = 321L)
log_sigma_grid <- seq(mode_eta[2] - 7 * grid_sd[2],
                      mode_eta[2] + 7 * grid_sd[2], length.out = 321L)
posterior_grid <- expand.grid(mu = mu_grid, log_sigma = log_sigma_grid)
posterior_grid$log_kernel <- apply(
  posterior_grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")], 1, log_posterior_eta
)
posterior_grid$weight <- exp(
  posterior_grid$log_kernel - log_sum_exp(posterior_grid$log_kernel)
)
posterior_grid$sigma <- exp(posterior_grid$log_sigma)

mu_mean <- sum(posterior_grid$mu * posterior_grid$weight)
sigma_mean <- sum(posterior_grid$sigma * posterior_grid$weight)
interval_probs <- seq(.025, .975, length.out = 3L)
mu_interval <- weighted_quantile(
  posterior_grid$mu, posterior_grid$weight, interval_probs
)
sigma_interval <- weighted_quantile(
  posterior_grid$sigma, posterior_grid$weight, interval_probs
)
probability_positive <- sum(
  posterior_grid$weight[posterior_grid$mu > 0]
)
boundary_mass <- sum(posterior_grid$weight[
  posterior_grid$mu %in% range(mu_grid) |
    posterior_grid$log_sigma %in% range(log_sigma_grid)
])

stopifnot(
  mode_fit$convergence == 0L,
  abs(sum(posterior_grid$weight) - 1) < 1e-12,
  boundary_mass < 1e-5
)

rbind(
  data.frame(parameter = "mu", mean = mu_mean,
             q025 = mu_interval[1], median = mu_interval[2],
             q975 = mu_interval[3]),
  data.frame(parameter = "sigma", mean = sigma_mean,
             q025 = sigma_interval[1], median = sigma_interval[2],
             q975 = sigma_interval[3])
)
```

### Riemann sums as area approximations {#riemann-sums-as-area-approximations}

An integral adds density over a continuous region. A **Riemann sum** replaces
that region with many small cells, evaluates the density at one point in each
cell, multiplies density height by cell area, and adds the resulting
approximate probability masses. In one dimension the cells are narrow
intervals; on this two-dimensional parameter grid they are rectangles with
area

$$
\Delta\mu\,\Delta\log\sigma.
$$

Thus an approximation to the normalizing integral is

$$
Z
\approx
\sum_{g}
\widetilde f(\eta_g\mid\mathbf y)
\Delta\mu\,\Delta\log\sigma,
$$

where $g$ indexes grid cells. Making the cells smaller tends to improve this
approximation when the density is sufficiently smooth and the grid covers the
region carrying appreciable mass.

The `321` by `321` grid has equal spacing in both coordinates, so every cell
has the same area. That common factor appears in both the numerator and the
sum used to normalize the weights, and therefore cancels. The normalized
weights can approximate posterior
[expectations](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#expectation-as-a-probability-weighted-average),
probability-weighted averages over the grid, even though the code does not
report the absolute value of $Z$.

### Sensitivity to the fixed tail parameter

The next calculation repeats the identical grid weighting with three
heavy-tailed likelihoods and a normal limit. We hold $\nu$ fixed at each
listed value and compare the resulting posteriors; we do not estimate $\nu$
from these calculations.

```{r}
#| label: check-provo-tail-sensitivity
summarize_tail_choice <- function(degrees) {
  log_kernel <- vapply(
    seq_len(nrow(posterior_grid)),
    function(index) {
      mu <- posterior_grid$mu[index]
      log_sigma <- posterior_grid$log_sigma[index]
      sigma <- exp(log_sigma)
      log_likelihood <- if (is.infinite(degrees)) {
        sum(dnorm(y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))
      } else {
        sum(
          dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = degrees, log = TRUE) -
            log(sigma)
        )
      }
      log_likelihood +
        dnorm(mu, 0, prior_mu_sd, log = TRUE) +
        log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_sigma_sd, log = TRUE) +
        log_sigma
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
  weight <- exp(log_kernel - log_sum_exp(log_kernel))
  data.frame(
    likelihood = if (is.infinite(degrees)) {
      "Normal limit"
    } else {
      paste0("Student-t, df = ", degrees)
    },
    mu_mean = sum(posterior_grid$mu * weight),
    probability_positive = sum(weight[posterior_grid$mu > 0]),
    boundary_mass = sum(weight[
      posterior_grid$mu %in% range(mu_grid) |
        posterior_grid$log_sigma %in% range(log_sigma_grid)
    ])
  )
}

tail_sensitivity <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(3, 4, 7, Inf), summarize_tail_choice) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
)
stopifnot(all(tail_sensitivity$boundary_mass < 1e-5))
tail_sensitivity
```

The boundary-mass column checks that reusing the same grid has not truncated one of the alternative targets. If these rows support materially different conclusions, fixing four degrees of freedom is carrying substantive weight. If they are similar, the reported location summary is less sensitive to this particular tail choice. Neither result establishes that the common symmetric location-scale model is correct.

The grid gives $\mathbb{P}(\mu>0\mid\mathbf y)=$ `r sprintf("%.3f", probability_positive)`, though the 95% interval for $\mu$, [`r sprintf("%.4f", mu_interval[1])`, `r sprintf("%.4f", mu_interval[3])`], includes zero. This measured result concerns the passage-level Student-t model only.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-raw-and-grid-fit
#| fig-cap: "Observed passage contrasts with the fitted Student-t density at the grid-posterior means."
density_grid <- data.frame(
  contrast = seq(min(y) - .04, max(y) + .04, length.out = 400L)
)
density_grid$density <- dt(
  (density_grid$contrast - mu_mean) / sigma_mean, df = nu
) / sigma_mean

ggplot(data.frame(contrast = y), aes(contrast)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 14,
                 fill = "grey78", color = "white") +
  geom_rug(color = "grey30") +
  geom_line(data = density_grid, aes(contrast, density),
            color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.85,
            inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Passage noun-minus-verb mean log first fixation duration",
       y = "Density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## The missing normalizer

The normalized posterior is

$$
f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)
=
\frac{\widetilde f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)}{Z},
\qquad
Z=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\widetilde f(\eta'\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\eta'.
$$

The grid approximates $Z$ numerically, but later algorithms need only relative density or its gradient. For two parameter values,

$$
\frac{f(\eta_b\mid\mathbf y)}{f(\eta_a\mid\mathbf y)}
=
\frac{\widetilde f(\eta_b\mid\mathbf y)}{\widetilde f(\eta_a\mid\mathbf y)},
$$

because $Z$ cancels. Thus we may still define the posterior when
$0<Z<\infty$ even if no closed-form expression for $Z$ is available. The
remaining problem is computational: we must approximate the required
integrals or ratios.

## Check your understanding

1. What does one $y_j$ summarize, and which lower-level observations have already been averaged away?
2. Why is `mean_log_ffd` not the log of an arithmetic mean duration?
3. Why does the passage-level Student-t model not support participant-level inference?
4. Which assumption permits the likelihood to factor over passages?
5. Why do we fix four degrees of freedom for this analysis, and what alternatives does the sensitivity calculation represent?
6. Which term is the Jacobian in the log target, and why does it appear?
7. Why does the normalized grid-weight calculation not need an explicit cell-area factor?
8. Why can later algorithms use the unnormalized target?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. One $y_j$ is a passage's mean noun log-FFD minus its mean verb log-FFD, computed from retained position summaries. Reader-level FFDs and word-position variation have already been averaged away. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The preparation first logs each positive reader-level duration and then averages those logged values. In general, $\overline{\log Y}\neq\log\overline Y$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Reader trials were already aggregated into position and passage summaries, so participant identities and participant-level variation cannot be recovered. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Conditional independence of the 55 passage contrasts, given $\mu$ and $\sigma$, permits the likelihood product. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The corpus does not determine four degrees of freedom. We fix four to retain finite variance and heavy tails while leaving only $\mu$ and $\sigma$ unknown; the sensitivity calculation compares heavier tails, lighter tails, and the normal limit. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
6. The final $+\log\sigma$ term is the Jacobian for the transformation $\sigma=\exp(\eta_2)$. It converts density on the positive $\sigma$ scale to density on the unconstrained $\log\sigma$ scale. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
7. Every grid point represents the same cell area, so that common factor cancels when the weights are normalized by their sum. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
8. Density ratios and gradients do not require the common normalizing constant $Z$; it cancels or differentiates away. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

## What carries forward

1. Each $y_j$ already averages over retained reader fixations and word positions. The posterior for $\mu$ therefore describes the center of 55 equally weighted passage contrasts, conditional on positive FFD, rather than a reader-level noun--verb effect.
2. The $t_4$ likelihood limits the influence of an extreme passage, while the data-calibrated priors place both parameters on the observed scale. Every later approximation inherits those modeling choices; changing the tail parameter, the aggregation, or the prior calibration changes the posterior target.
3. Likelihood times priors gives an integrable kernel. The grid converts that kernel into normalized weights, and the Jacobian appears only because the computation expresses positive $\sigma$ through $\log\sigma$. Later algorithms may avoid evaluating $Z$ explicitly because ratios or gradients remove the common constant, but they still target the same density.

The [Monte Carlo page](monte-carlo-integration.qmd#from-a-weighted-sum-to-a-draw-average) next uses independent draws from this normalized grid to approximate posterior expectations. A reader-by-word hierarchical model remains a live possibility. It would retain variation removed by the passage summaries, while also changing both the inferential target and the computational problem.
